title: Numeric Data, Precision, Rounding, and Range
learningObjectives: Distinguish integer and fractional numeric values and their typical uses.
Explain precision, accuracy, and rounding at a basic level.
Recognize that numeric representations have finite ranges and limits.
Describe why floating-point calculations can produce unexpected decimal results.
Choose appropriate rounding and range checks for a task.

understand.concept: Numeric data represents quantities using integer or fractional forms. Computers store numbers using finite representations, so some values cannot be represented exactly. Precision describes the detail or resolution available; accuracy describes closeness to the intended or true value. Rounding changes a value to a chosen level of detail, while range limits define the values a representation or application can handle.
understand.whyItMatters: Numeric assumptions can affect money, measurements, averages, graphics, counters, scientific calculations, and input validation. Understanding representation limits prevents incorrect comparisons, overflow-like problems, misleading display values, and inappropriate rounding.
understand.analogy: A measuring ruler with marks every centimeter cannot show every tiny fraction exactly. A digital representation also has limits in how finely it can represent values, although the specific limits depend on its numeric format.
understand.analogyLimit: Numeric behavior varies by language and data type. Integer overflow, decimal arithmetic, rounding modes, and floating-point precision differ; financial calculations often need decimal or integer-minor-unit strategies.

explain.narrative: Integers are suited to whole counts and index values; fractional numeric types are used for measurements and calculations involving decimals. Floating-point formats represent many decimal fractions approximately. A calculation such as 0.1 + 0.2 may therefore produce a value very close to—but not exactly—0.3. Avoid relying on exact equality for approximate calculations; compare within a tolerance when appropriate. Rounding should generally be applied for display or according to a deliberate domain rule, not casually after every intermediate calculation. Always consider the permitted range and units.

examples.title: Integer count
examples.explanation: A whole number is suitable for a count of items; a fractional count would not make sense for this context.

examples.title: Floating-point approximation
examples.explanation: Binary floating-point cannot represent some decimal fractions exactly, so the displayed result may contain a tiny approximation.

examples.title: Compare using a tolerance
examples.explanation: A tolerance expresses how close is acceptable for an approximate measurement rather than requiring exact equality.

examples.title: Round for display
examples.explanation: This example rounds to two decimal places for presentation. The domain's rounding policy should be chosen deliberately.

examples.title: Check a valid range
examples.code: const temperature = 23; const accepted = temperature >= -50 && temperature <= 60;
examples.explanation: The application validates that the numeric value lies inside an expected range; units and context must also be known.

commonMistakes: Expecting every decimal fraction to be stored exactly.
Using exact equality for floating-point results when approximation is expected.
Rounding repeatedly during intermediate calculations without a policy.
Ignoring units, valid range, or overflow limitations.
Assuming a display-rounded value is the same as the stored numeric value.
